---
title: "Time stepping and the field driver"
---

The viscoelastic evolution is an **explicit** march in time built directly on
the elastic operator. This page covers how a step is taken, how the memory state
is carried, and how the field-level driver feeds the
[sea-level equation](../physics/sea-level.qmd) without corrupting that state.

## One step

The $\omega=1$ Maxwell scheme (see [Rheology](../physics/rheology.qmd)) keeps the
left-hand operator fixed and updates only the right-hand side. A step at degree
$j$ is:

1. Form the dissipative forcing $-\int\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1}:\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$
   from the *previous* memory stress (a two-point radial Gauss quadrature of the
   spectral double-dot over the four spheroidal tensor components).
2. Add the surface-load right-hand side for the current load.
3. **Back-substitute** through the once-factored operator (no re-factorization).
4. Update the memory stress
   $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} = (1-M)\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1} - 2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i}$
   from the new strain.

Elastic layers ($M\to 0$) freeze; fluid layers ($\mu=0$) carry no memory. The
1D validation `test_relax` shows a held load relaxing monotonically from the
elastic Love number to the fluid limit $-(2j+1)/3$, with $t_{\text{relax}}\propto\eta$
and convergence under step refinement.

This explicit update is **conditionally stable**: the step is capped by the
shortest Maxwell time, so a short dynamical $\Delta t$ is sub-cycled within the
coupling interval. The `vilma_timestep` controller sizes the sub-steps
according to the memory scheme (see [Rheology](../physics/rheology.qmd#memory-time-schemes)):

- **`"fe"`** (default): the 1st-order update has no embedded error signal, so
  $\Delta t$ is set *a priori* by the stability ceiling $M = \mu\Delta t/\eta \le$
  `cfl` (default 1), taken over the fastest Maxwell rate present. The interval
  is split into equal sub-steps of at most that length. `dt_max` lowers the
  sub-step further. `dt_min` raises it, also above the stability ceiling, so
  it should stay at its default of 0 (none) for this scheme. A guard rolls a
  sub-step back and halves it if the memory norm becomes non-finite or grows
  more than $10^{3}$-fold. It is a safety net and normally never fires.
- **`"trap"`**: each candidate step is taken once at $\Delta t$ and once as two
  $\Delta t/2$ halves. Their difference estimates the local error of the
  memory, which is compared with `atol` $+$ `rtol` $\times$ the memory norm
  (defaults $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-4}$). A rejected step is rolled back and
  retried smaller. An accepted one keeps the fine result. The next step size
  follows from the error estimate with the factor `safety` (0.9). Its change
  is limited to between `shrink_min` (0.2) and `grow_max` (5), and its value
  to the range `dt_min`–`dt_max`. A step at `dt_min` is accepted even above
  tolerance. The first trial step is `dt_init` (default 0: the whole
  interval). The step size then carries over from one interval to the next.

The `dt_*` parameters are given in years. The coupling interval itself is not
a parameter: the host, or the forcing time axis of the standalone driver,
passes it with each update. The ice load is interpolated linearly between the
interval endpoints. `scheme = "etd1"` follows the `"fe"` path here and
`scheme = "be"` the `"trap"` path (see
[Rheology](../physics/rheology.qmd#memory-time-schemes)).

## The viscoelastic field driver

The SLE needs a *field* load whose every coefficient $(\ell,m)$ has its **own
independent load history** — the ice and ocean evolve differently everywhere.
The `ve_response` driver provides this while remaining safe to call from inside
an iterative solver, using the **affine** structure of the response at fixed
time:

$$
u_{\ell m} \;=\; g_u(\ell)\,\sigma_{\ell m} \;+\; \text{drift}_{\ell m},
$$

where $g_u(\ell)$ is the instantaneous (elastic) gain and $\text{drift}_{\ell m}$
comes from the *frozen* past-relaxation memory. The step is bracketed:

- **`begin_step`** freezes the drift — one memory-forcing solve per coefficient,
  done once at the start of the step;
- `apply()` is then a cheap affine evaluation the SLE fixed point may call
  repeatedly;
- the **memory advance** then moves the Maxwell memory forward once, with the
  converged load.

The memory advance has two entry points. `commit_step` takes a given load and
is used by the response-level tests. The sea-level solve instead uses
`prepare_endpoint`, `advance_endpoint` and `finalize_step`, which let the load
and the memory converge together. With `scheme = "fe"` both do one explicit
update. With `scheme = "trap"` the update needs the end-of-step strain, so the
step endpoint is iterated: the drift is re-solved against the trial
$\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i}$ until the surface drift stops changing (relative
change below $10^{-6}$). In the sea-level solve the water load is re-converged
in each of these passes, up to `sle_max_mem_iter` passes (default 20).
`max_couple_iter` caps the passes of `commit_step` only, so it does not affect
a model run.

Each complex $(\ell,m)$ history is stored as two real histories (real/imaginary),
since the operator and $M=\mu\Delta t/\eta$ are real. The per-element Maxwell
kernel is shared verbatim with the 1D stepper — `test_ve_response` confirms the
field driver's first step equals `elastic_response` exactly, and that a held
degree-2 field reproduces the 1D `ve_degree` history to $\sim 10^{-13}$.

## Memory storage and restart

The per-$(\ell,m)$ memory and drift are stored in **degree-grouped slot order**
(an $\ell m \leftrightarrow k$ map), so the inner loop is contiguous *and*
per-degree, allowing operator reuse without scattering the (large) memory arrays.

A restart file is written without rounding. It carries the following state:

| State | Variables | Carried when |
|---|---|---|
| Maxwell memory stress, four spheroidal channels or six with the [toroidal field](../physics/toroidal.qmd) | `tau_*` | viscoelastic response |
| start-of-step load of the trapezoidal scheme, and its flag | `sigma_n_*`, `sigma_primed` | viscoelastic response |
| model time | `time` | always |
| next trial step of the step controller | `dt_try_s` | always |
| polar motion and the memory of both degree-2 channels | `rot_m_*`, `rot_load_mem`, `rot_tidal_mem` | [rotation](../physics/rotation.qmd) on |
| host-resolved terms of the last update (the start of the next ramp) | `w_prev`, `I_g_prev`, `C_prev`, `F_prev` | host-resolved terms |
| surface fields of the last update: ice, relative sea level and its two parts, bed, ocean function, barystatic scalars | `h_ice`, `rsl`, `dz_bed`, `dz_ss`, `z_bed`, `C_ocean`, `bsl`, … | always |

The memory stress is by far the largest part. The surface fields follow from
the memory and the load, but they are restored as well: the ice is the start
of the next load ramp, and the relative sea level seeds the next sea-level
solve. The elastic and the null response carry no memory, so their restart
holds the other rows only. The full variable table is `input/vilma-variables.md`.

The reference fields are static: the equilibrium bed and ice and, with
host-resolved terms, the host reference. They are written once and compared
with the initialized model on read. A mismatch stops the run. A file with
host-resolved terms cannot be read into a run without them, nor the reverse.

A restart also records the Earth its memory belongs to: checksums of the
radial mesh (`mesh_checksum`), of the radial viscosity (`visc_radial_checksum`)
and of the 3-D field (`visc_3d_checksum`). A restart from another mesh is
refused. A restart from another viscosity is refused too, unless
`restart_other_visc = .true.` (`&ctl`): its memory then seeds the run (e.g. a
1-D spin-up for a 3-D run) rather than continuing it. Other parameters (the
time scheme, the sea-level settings) are not checked.

A run resumes at the restart's time. The driver starts the forcing window at
that time, and a `time_init` that selects another start stops the run, so a
restart cannot replay the forcing by mistake. `restart_time_reset = .true.`
(`&ctl`) instead takes the restart's state as the state at the start of the
window, whatever time the file carries.

`test_restart` asserts that a restarted run reproduces an uninterrupted one
**bit for bit**, with rotation on, for a radially symmetric Earth and for a
3-D field with toroidal channels. `test_restart_3d` asserts the same after the
1-D pre-spin-up, and `test_restart_host` covers host-resolved terms.

A lower-resolution restart can be read into a higher-resolution run. The
memory of the shared low degrees is copied (a contiguous block in the
degree-grouped order) and the higher degrees start at zero. The surface
fields, the trapezoidal load and the host-resolved terms live on the file's
grid and are not transferred. The caller re-derives the surface fields with a
zero-length update. A run can thus be spun up at coarse resolution and
continued at fine resolution, but that continuation is not bit for bit. A
higher-resolution file cannot be read into a lower-resolution run.

## Coupling cadence

For host coupling (CLIMBER-X), the model sub-cycles its short dynamical step
$\Delta t$ within a longer coupling interval. The ice thickness ramps linearly
from the previous update's value to the new one across the interval. The SLE
is solved each $\Delta t$, and the bedrock
$z_{\text{bed}} = z_{\text{bed,eq}} - \text{rsl}$ is returned at the coupling
cadence.

The reference state is the relaxed state. The memory is zero there, and
relative sea level is measured against it. A host passes the reference at
initialization. The standalone driver chooses it with `i_eq` (`&ctl`):

| `i_eq` | Reference bed and ice |
|---|---|
| 0 | the start slice of the forcing |
| 1 (default) | a present-day reference (`z_bed_ref_file`, `h_ice_ref_file`), so that rsl is close to zero at the present day |
| 2 | an equilibrium state read from `z_bed_eq_file` and `h_ice_eq_file` |
| 3 | the present-day reference bed plus an rsl field from `rsl_restart_file` |

### Spin-up

A run that starts away from the reference (a held LGM load, say) starts with
zero memory, as if the load had just been applied. The optional **spin-up**
(`solid_earth_spinup`) removes this. It holds the start-slice ice and relaxes
the model toward isostatic equilibrium, with the reference kept as the datum.
The transient then starts with viscous memory. The spin-up has two phases,
both off by default:

- **Full-model phase** (`equil_time_max` $> 0$, in years). The held load is
  relaxed in passes of growing length: 200 yr first, then 1.6 times longer
  each pass, at most 60 passes. After each pass the mean bed velocity is the
  global mean of the absolute bed change over the pass, divided by the pass
  length. The phase ends when this falls below `equil_rate_tol` (default
  $10^{-3}$ m/yr). `equil_time_max` caps the total relaxation time. If the cap
  is reached first, the run continues and prints a warning with the remaining
  rate.
- **1-D pre-phase** (`pre_spinup_1d = .true.`). The same relaxation first runs
  on a laterally uniform field, the lateral mean of $\log_{10}\eta$ of the 3-D
  field at each radius. It uses the same convergence test and has no time
  cap. The 3-D field is then restored and the memory is kept. This phase is
  cheap, because no element is on the 3-D path. It is independent of
  `equil_time_max`.

The rate of each pass is measured over exactly that pass's memory advance.
The criterion is a global mean. It bounds the mean bed velocity, not the
velocity at every point, and it is not a measure of how far the relaxation has
gone. In a test with a held cap load on a 500 kyr relaxation, the default
`equil_rate_tol` of $10^{-3}$ m/yr stops at about 83 % of the full relaxation.
The default thus gives a reference that is close to, but not at, isostatic
equilibrium. For a fully relaxed reference, lower `equil_rate_tol` (by an
order of magnitude or more) and raise `equil_time_max` accordingly, at the cost
of a longer spin-up. Elements with very high viscosity do not equilibrate
within any practical cap, which is what the
[lid rule](../physics/rheology.qmd#visc3d-input) addresses. `test_spinup`
asserts that the spin-up relaxes the held load well beyond a single cold
step, and that the state after it is near-stationary. The spin-up is not
available with `solver = "v1"`.

A zero-length update (`dt = 0`) advances neither time nor memory. It solves
the sea-level equation under the ice it is handed, against the current memory,
and refreshes the surface fields, so relative sea level, the ocean function and
`h_ice` describe the same ice. It is idempotent: a second call with the same
ice changes nothing. The spin-up begins with one, and a run without spin-up (a
restarted run included) begins with one, to seed the start-slice ice. A
negative `dt` stops the run.

::: {.callout-tip title="Where this lives in the code"}
`vilma_viscoelastic` (1D stepper + shared kernel), `vilma_response` (`ve_response`
field driver, `begin_step`/`commit_step`), `vilma_io` (netCDF restart), and
`vilma_coupling` (host init/update contract, spin-up), `vilma_timestep` (the
sub-step controller) and `vilma_sle` (the load–memory iteration). The cost of
the drift solve in `begin_step` is addressed in [Solver](solver.qmd).
:::
